tagline.text: A clear lake filling the crater of the T'boli people's sacred mountain

budget.label: Budget

children.text: A mountain lake at about 1,280m elevation, filling the crater left by the 1641 eruption of Mount Melibengoy (Parker). It has been named the Philippines' cleanest inland body of water, and reaching it means a 3–6 hour trek with a T'boli guide, then camping on the shore.
Lake Holon (also called Lake Maughan) is the crater lake of Mount Melibengoy (formerly Mount Parker), a mountain rising out of the highlands of T'boli, South Cotabato. The lake surface sits at about
above sea level, ringed by a caldera wall roughly
2.9km
across and 200–500m tall, creating a scene like blue water poured into a giant green bowl. The volcano's highest point stands about
above sea level.
The lake was formed by a massive eruption of Mount Melibengoy in
January 1641

. The eruption was so large that some studies suggest it affected East Asia's climate at the time, and rainwater later collected in the crater to form the lake seen today. It was named the Philippines' cleanest inland body of water in both
and
, and the area around the lake is protected as part of the Allah Valley Protected Landscape.
Mount Melibengoy and Lake Holon are sacred sites, home to ancestral spirits, for the
T'boli

, the indigenous people of this land. Tourism is jointly managed by the T'boli municipal government and the local community, and visitors must register and enter with a local guide. To let the ecosystem around the lake recover, it closes to visitors for about two months at the start of every year; in
, too, it was closed from
January 3
through
March
Reaching the lake takes about
3–4 hours
on the relatively gentle Salacafe trail, or about
5–6 hours

on the Kule trail, which has better views. Once there, you pitch a tent on the shore and spend the time with a misty dawn lake and a night full of stars. There are almost no amenities, but in exchange the nature remains relatively untouched, making it widely regarded as southern Mindanao's finest destination for travelers who love camping and trekking.
Follow the Kule trail and you'll reach a viewpoint rock at the caldera's edge that offers the classic view of the whole lake at once. Time your arrival for a clear morning.
Pitching a tent at the designated lakeshore campground for the night is the heart of a Holon trip. Temperatures drop sharply after sunset, and on a clear night, stars fill the sky above the caldera.
At sunrise, mist rises off the lake and the caldera wall slowly reveals itself — a gift only those who camp overnight get to see. Sit by the shore with a warm coffee and take it in.
You can rent a kayak or raft run by the local community and drift across the calm water. The water is clear enough to see the bottom near the edges.

blocks.title: Swimming and a natural fish spa

children.text: You can dip into the cold lake water in permitted areas, and in the shallows, small fish nibbling at your feet give you a natural fish spa.

blocks.title: Kissing Stone and the forest trail

children.text: Pass sights scattered along the forest trail, including the Salacafe trail's famous Kissing Stone (two rocks touching each other), while spotting moss-covered trees, pitcher plants, and wild orchids.
Most guides and porters are T'boli locals. Hearing the legends and traditions tied to the mountain and lake as you walk makes the scenery feel even richer.

Registration and guide assignment happen at the T'boli tourism office or a designated registration point, so don't head straight to the trailhead — register first, following the instructions.
The
Salacafe trail
is relatively gentle, taking about
3–4 hours
, and is popular with beginners or as a descent route. The
Kule trail
takes about
5–6 hours
and is tougher, but passes the caldera viewpoint rock for the most famous view.
A traverse itinerary, going up via Kule and down via Salacafe, is popular. Which trails operate and visitor limits can change, so check the latest notices.

March–May

June–October
brings frequent afternoon rain, turning trails muddy, and on many days fog blocks the view of the lake. The lakeshore up the mountain stays cool during the day at around

at night and dawn, feeling even colder with wind. The rest period and reopening dates change every year, so be sure to check the latest notices from the T'boli tourism office.

At the lake, the standard is to camp in a tent at the designated campground. There are sometimes simple huts or shelters run by the community, but they're few and basic, so it's safer to bring your own tent and sleeping bag. Before and after the trek, it's convenient to stay at a simple inn in T'boli town (about
a night) or a lakeside resort at nearby Lake Sebu (about

There are no shops on the mountain, so buy food such as rice, canned goods, vegetables, eggs, and coffee at the market in T'boli town and bring it with you. Guides sometimes cook rice and grill food at the lakeshore, so discuss meal arrangements before you set out. If you stop at Lake Sebu after descending, be sure to try grilled and fried tilapia raised in the lake, along with traditional T'boli food.

Before you go, check whether the lake is open, the registration process, and fees through the T'boli tourism office's official social media or by phone. There is no way in during the rest period, under any circumstances.
You need to leave General Santos early in the morning to reach the lake by that afternoon. For a more relaxed pace, stay overnight in Koronadal or T'boli the day before.
Nights are chilly, so bring a warm jacket, a sleeping bag, and spare socks. It's best to pack everything in waterproof bags.
The trail has a lot of dirt and roots, becoming very slippery in the rain. Good-grip hiking boots and trekking poles are recommended.
Cell signal is weak on most of the mountain and trail. Let your family know your itinerary and your guide's contact number.
Going up via Kule and down via Salacafe gets you both the views and an easier pace on the way down.
Combining this with nearby Lake Sebu after descending lets you enjoy T'boli culture and Seven Falls too.

Lake Holon is both a sacred T'boli site and a protected area. Never enter without registering and a guide, and since security conditions in the mountainous areas of South Cotabato can also change, be sure to check your home country's latest travel advisories and the local tourism office's notices.
A magnitude 7.8 earthquake off Sarangani on
June 8, 2026
triggered landslides on Mount Melibengoy and the Salacafe course, and the DENR Region 12 office suspended visits and trekking to Lake Holon until further notice. Earlier, in
April
, the lake also closed for about
2 weeks
because of fighting between the army and rebels in a nearby village, so make your plans only after confirming reopening and safety notices.
Avoid using soap, shampoo, or detergent that would pollute the lake water, and carry out all your trash, including food waste.
Swim only where your guide permits. The lake gets deep just past the edge, and the water is very cold.
Since this is a sacred site, avoid loud noise, drunken disturbances, and imitating rituals without permission, and follow your guide's instructions.
Heavy rain can wash out the trail or swell valley streams. If your guide suggests changing the plan, follow their lead.
Trekking after dark is very dangerous. Set out early enough to reach the lake or trailhead by early afternoon at the latest.
